newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Tycoon Tung chosen Hong Kong post-handover leader.
newsitem.headline: Tycoon Tung chosen Hong Kong post-handover leader.

text.p: Shipping magnate Tung Chee-hwa swept effortlessly to a historic victory on Wednesday in the poll to select Hong Kong's leader-in-waiting to take over when the British colony reverts to Chinese rule next year.
A 400-strong Selection Committee, carefully assembled by Beijing, voted overwhelmingly as expected for the 59-year-old businessman, whose family maritime empire was bailed out by China a decade ago.
Tung declared his victory, considered a foregone conclusion in Hong Kong for weeks, a triumph not just for himself but for the entire Chinese nation.

"For the past 100 years, Hong Kong has been a colony. Now we are in charge of ourselves. I believe most Hong Kong people have confidence in the future," he said in a victory speech that stressed the need for stability and downplayed democracy.

Hong Kong's pro-democracy lobby, which dismissed the ballot as a travesty and boycotted the process, demonstrated outside the hall where the vote took place in a ceremony redolent of events in Beijing's Great Hall of the People.

Activists screaming "oppose the phoney election" scuffled with riot police and one of Hong Kong's best-known pro-democracy politicians, Emily Lau, was arrested and dragged away kicking and screaming for her part in the protest.
Lau had scheduled a no-confidence debate on the future leadership in the Legislative Council later in the day. She was released on bail ahead of the event.
China's foreign minister, Qian Qichen, who presided over the ballot that he described as the birth of democracy in Hong Kong, was the first to congratulate the future leader.
"We would like to congratulate Mr Tung," Qian, making only his second trip to Hong Kong, told the electoral panel.
Tung collected 320 votes. His nearest rival, former chief justice Yang Ti Liang, took only 42. The third contender, businessman Peter Woo, polled 36, and two votes were spoiled.
Hong Kong Governor Chris Patten congratulated the man who will succeed him when more than 150 years of British colonial rule passes into the history books next year.
Patten pledged assistance in the months ahead as Tung begins to assemble the team that will take over when Britain hands its last Asian outpost to China at midnight next June 30.

When July 1 dawns, the red flag of China will flutter over the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region of China, a quasi-autonomous territory that China has promised can maintain its capitalist freedoms for 50 years.
"I wish Mr Tung every success in his endeavour and I have congratulated him personally," Patten said of Tung, who resigned from Patten's inner cabinet of advisers to contest the post.
Taipei also added its voice to a long string of congratulatory messages that flowed in from overseas.

The two defeated contenders were quick to offer their congratulations to Tung, a reclusive tycoon who valued his privacy but will no longer be able to habitally drive himself to functions and take taxis to his office.
Tung's personal assistant, Stanley Shen, said bodyguards would be assigned permanently from now on.

Tung was due to depart later on Wednesday for Shenzhen, a Chinese special economic zone across the border from Hong Kong, where he was expected to receive China's official blessing as Hong Kong's chief executive-designate.
